Neonatal specimens of the Mediterranean starry ray (Raja asterias) emerge from their egg cases at a remarkably consistent size, with field measurements indicating a total length at birth of 10.6 cm [Lb = 10.6 cm]. This modest size at parturition is typical for small-to-medium-sized skates and reflects the finite yolk reserves available to the developing embryo within the tough, fibrous egg capsule. The yolk-dependent embryo undergoes a protracted incubation period, the duration of which is strongly influenced by ambient temperature. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 14.3 °C [T = 14.3 °C], hatching occurs after approximately 150 days [ab = approximately 150 days], a developmental span that is consistent with the slow metabolic rates characteristic of many rajiform species at cool to moderate thermal regimes. This lengthy embryogenesis ensures that pups are relatively well-developed at emergence, with fully formed claspers in males and a robust, flattened body plan suited for benthic life. The seasonal timing of egg deposition in the Mediterranean thus likely ensures that neonates encounter favorable environmental conditions for their subsequent growth and survival.

As the young rays grow and transition through their juvenile phase, they undergo a period of sustained somatic expansion that culminates in the attainment of a maximum adult body size. The ultimate total length recorded for this species reaches 75 cm [Li = 75 cm], a value that places Raja asterias among the medium-sized skate fauna of the Mediterranean basin. This asymptotic length is reached only after several years of steady growth, during which the sub-adult individuals progressively shift from a diet dominated by small crustaceans to one incorporating larger prey such as teleost fishes and cephalopods. Concomitant with this increase in linear dimensions, the maximum wet weight achieved by fully grown adults can approach 3100 grams [Wwi = 3100 grams], a mass that reflects both the allometric scaling of body volume and the accumulation of lipid reserves in the liver, which is critical for buoyancy control and energy storage. This ultimate wet weight is derived from a length-weight relationship typical of the genus and underscores the substantial biomass these rays represent in their coastal benthic communities.

Reproductive maturation in the Mediterranean starry ray follows a distinct pattern, with males typically attaining sexual maturity at a smaller size than females. Detailed morphometric surveys indicate that the total length at puberty for males is 50 cm [Lp = 50 cm], whereas the combined population-level estimate for both sexes, reflecting the onset of gonadal activity, centers around 54 cm [Lp = around 54 cm]. This difference suggests that male rays begin producing viable spermatozoa and developing functional claspers at a slightly smaller body size than the size at which females initiate ovarian maturation and vitellogenesis. The onset of puberty in both sexes is accompanied by pronounced changes in the relative dimensions of the reproductive organs, including the enlargement of the testes and the development of the oviducal glands in females. These size-based thresholds are critical for fisheries management, as they define the minimum size at which individuals can contribute to the next generation and thus inform the design of size limits or mesh regulations aimed at protecting the spawning stock from overexploitation.

The maximum reproductive rate of Raja asterias is constrained by both its life history strategy and the thermal environment it inhabits. Based on comparative data from other Raja species kept under controlled conditions at 14.3 °C [T = 14.3 °C], the estimated maximum reproductive rate is approximately 20 offspring per year. This annual output is achieved through the continuous production of small clutches of eggs throughout the year, rather than a single, large seasonal batch, with females laying one or two encapsulated ova per spawning event [N_R_i = one or two encapsulated ova per spawning event] and producing approximately 10 to 20 such events per year [F_R_i = approximately 10 to 20 such events per year]. The modest fecundity relative to many teleost fishes reflects the energetic investment per offspring, as each egg case provides substantial yolk reserves and a protective capsule that reduces early-life mortality. This life history tactic, characterized by relatively low fecundity and extended parental investment in the form of yolk provision, is typical of elasmobranchs and renders populations vulnerable to overfishing if adult mortality rates increase.

Longevity represents a key axis of the starry ray's life history, and available records from tag-recapture studies conducted at a mean ambient temperature of 14.3 °C [T = 14.3 °C] suggest that the maximum lifespan for this species extends to approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years]. This relatively short lifespan compared to larger, deeper-water skate species is consistent with its moderate body size, early maturation, and the relatively high metabolic demands imposed by its warm-temperate Mediterranean habitat. Individuals that survive the high juvenile mortality associated with predation by piscivorous fish and marine mammals can complete their entire life cycle within this five-year window, progressing from a 10.6 cm [Lb = 10.6 cm] neonate to a sexually mature adult and producing several generations of offspring. The species' physiological decline with senescence is marked by a gradual reduction in reproductive output and an increased susceptibility to parasitic infections, culminating in natural mortality after the completion of the reproductive lifespan. This compressed generation time, combined with its moderate fecundity, shapes the demographic resilience of Raja asterias to both natural environmental variability and anthropogenic pressures such as bottom trawling and habitat degradation.
